cases.evidence: Page source (case-06.html L23-24): `.body-copy a { color: #3366CC; text-decoration: none; }` and `.body-copy a:hover, .body-copy a:focus-visible { text-decoration: underline; }` on `body { background:#fff; color:#000 }`. I recomputed the contrasts from the hex values: relative luminance of #3366CC = 0.1457, so link-vs-black-body-text = (0.1457+0.05)/0.05 = 3.91:1 and link-vs-white-background = 1.05/0.1957 = 5.37:1 — exactly the figures the corpus claims. The page is the literal G183 worked example, and the hover/focus underline required by G183's second Expected Result is present.
cases.reasoning: Ajit's comment is specific and intelligible but appeals to a house rule ('our strict 1.4.1 testing parameters') that WCAG itself does not impose: G183 permits colour-only-looking links when the link-vs-text lightness contrast is at least 3:1 AND an additional visual cue appears on hover/focus. Both conditions hold here (3.91:1 plus the hover/focus underline), so the corpus's `passed` label is right and the complaint is a judgment disagreement the rationale already answers. The only quibble worth recording is a framing nuance the pipeline self-review already logged: the mechanism prose says the page 'does not depend on the hover/focus underline', whereas G183's formal procedure requires that cue too — but the page supplies it, so nothing about the label changes.

cases.evidence: result.json (aspectResults[dismissible-position-obscures-meaningful-vs-decorative].built.pages[case-04]) says expected='passed', primarySelector='#al-cacio', scenario='Restaurant menu ... decorative olive-branch SVG flourish (aria-hidden)'. The shipped page is <title>Trail Conditions | Larkspur Ridge Open Space</title>; `grep -rl al-cacio eval/` matches only metadata files, and `flourish` appears nowhere except result.json. The case's own doc (case-04.md, title line and 'Expected ACT-style outcome') states '**failed** — additional content shown on hover/focus obscures an *informational* graphic (the difficulty key) and there is no dismiss mechanism'. Probe: `probe-case.js case-04.html --hover button.help` -> tooltip `.tip.is-open` visible at {x:338,y:159,w:300,h:229}, hoverableAfterPointerTravel=true, visibleTooltipsAfterEscape=1 (Esc does NOT dismiss; the source has no keydown handler). Screenshot confirms the open tooltip covers the 'Difficulty key' heading, the whole `.key` legend row, and the first trail's marker+name.
cases.reasoning: The page on disk is not the page the source of truth describes, and the two disagree on the outcome: result.json/manifest say `passed` (decorative carve-out) while the shipped page plus its own .md are a deliberately constructed FAIL (tooltip obscures an informational legend, no Esc). Davin's issueExists=yes matches the page as shipped. Repair therefore requires flipping `expected` from passed to failed and rewriting scenario/mechanism/whyAutomatedToolsMiss/primarySelector to the Larkspur Ridge fixture (primarySelector `#cond`, trigger `button.help`), which is out of bounds for a mechanical fix. Note the corpus's own DRIFT-REPORT.md line 63 already flags this exact case as not-aligned, so a human decision is the only missing step; also note this aspect loses its decorative-carve-out PASS control if the label flips (case-03 remains as the white-space PASS control).

cases.evidence: case-02.html L31-60: `<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" role="img" aria-describedby="chartCap" aria-label="Bar chart of FY2029 freight division revenue by quarter">` with bars $42M/$48M/$55M and a red (#c0362c) Q4 bar of $19M plus an on-chart `<text ... fill="#c0362c">↓ port strike</text>`. The referenced description (L62-66) reads in full: 'Q1 revenue was $42M, Q2 revenue was $48M, Q3 revenue was $55M, and Q4 revenue was $19M. All four quarters are shown above.' It states no trend, does not identify Q4 as the outlier, and never mentions the 'port strike' annotation. Because the SVG carries role="img", its child <text> nodes are pruned from the accessibility tree, so the annotation is available to sighted users only.
cases.reasoning: Mengqi filed issueExists=no with an empty comment body — no specifics to act on. Checking the page myself, information the image conveys ('↓ port strike', and which quarter is the anomaly) is genuinely absent from the programmatic description, which is the F67 pattern the corpus claims; the `failed` label stands and Ajit's approval is the correct read. Separate observation (not the annotator's complaint, and not scored here): the shipped page still contains a visible `aside.note` beginning 'Why automated checkers pass this page:' that spells out the answer in rendered text — the comment strip removed HTML comments but left this leak.

cases.evidence: case-03.html L23 `.bring li::before { content:"•"; color:#c0392b; ... }` and L30 `.f.req label::before { content:"•"; color:#c0392b; ... }` — the required marker and the decorative checklist marker are the same glyph in the SAME hex colour. L46 legend: 'Fields marked with a red dot are required. All other fields are optional.' Screenshot (probe --shot) confirms: the five required labels each carry a red dot, the three optional labels (Pronouns / Preferred pharmacy / Relationship to patient) carry none, and the decorative dots live in a separately boxed 'What to bring to your appointment' list above the form, next to prose items that are not form fields.
cases.reasoning: The corpus mechanism asserts that 'hue is the sole disambiguator' between the required marker and the decorative bullet — but both bullets are rendered in the identical colour #c0392b, so hue cannot be doing any distinguishing work; what separates them is position/context (form label vs. checklist item), and that cue survives grayscale intact. Independently, required-vs-optional is signalled by presence/absence of the bullet, a non-colour visual means, which is what SC 1.4.1 actually asks for. Mengqi's bare 'no-error' is weak evidence on its own, but my own reading of the page finds the failure argument self-undermining, so the `failed` label is genuinely in question. A defensible counter-argument survives (the legend identifies the marker by colour word, 'a red dot'), so this is a ground-truth call for a human, not a mechanical fix. The pipeline self-review separately recorded that the .md's claim that the ::before bullet is 'invisible to AT entirely' is refuted by the Chromium AX tree.

cases.evidence: case-06.html L30-31: `<svg role="img" aria-describedby="waterTable waterTrend" aria-label="Bar chart of Marsden residential water use, 2025 to 2029">`; #waterTable (L61-73) lists 2025 13.8 / 2026 12.9 / 2027 12.1 / 2028 11.0 / 2029 10.2, matching every bar label in the SVG, and #waterTrend (L75-79) states the direction, the 26% total reduction and the largest single-year drop (1.1 bn L, 2027->2028). Substituting table + trend paragraph for the image loses nothing (G92 satisfied).
cases.reasoning: There is no complaint to adjudicate: both annotators answered issueExists=no, which agrees with the corpus label `passed`, and Mengqi's 'no-error' comment body is empty. The case only entered the batch because a comment was attached with no text. Verifying the page myself, the description genuinely reconstructs the chart, so the PASS control is sound. Same leak note as case-02: the visible `aside.note` 'Why this page PASSES (control):' remains in the served HTML.

cases.evidence: `probe-case.js case-01.html --hover "#limitHelp"` reports the revealed tooltip at rect {x:500, y:1170, w:280, h:150} — roughly 950px BELOW the trigger, which sits at about y=222 on a page whose real content ends near y=560 (see full-page screenshot: nothing appears next to the '?' button; the 1320px page height is itself produced by the stranded tooltip). hoverableAfterPointerTravel=false. Root cause is in the source: `.tip { position:absolute; left:50%; top:130%; ... }` (L28-29) but `#limitTip` (L58) is a child of the static `<form>`; the only `position:relative` in the file is on `.help` (L20), the sibling <button>, so the tooltip resolves its percentages against the initial containing block (left 50% of 1280 -> 640-140=500; top 130% of the 900px viewport -> 1170).
cases.reasoning: Davin's 'nothing pops up for the user' is exactly right as an observation of rendered behaviour: the tooltip does get class 'show', but it paints ~1000px away from its trigger, off the visible page. This is a page-implementation bug (a missing positioning context), not a ground-truth question — the documented Persistent defect is in the JS and is untouched by the repair, so `expected` stays 'failed'. I applied the patch below to a scratch copy and re-probed: the tooltip then renders at {x:203, y:260} directly under the '?' button, hoverableAfterPointerTravel=true, Esc dismisses it, and a timed check confirms the documented failure survives (opacity 1 / visible at t=0.5s, opacity 0 / hidden at t=4.7s while the pointer is still on the trigger). The patch also stops the tooltip text and the trigger's aria-label from leaking into the accessible name of #amt, since they no longer sit inside its <label>. Note the corpus's own drift check marked this case 'aligned' because it read the source rather than the rendering, so this defect is new.

proposedFix.rationale: Give the tooltip a positioning context adjacent to its trigger. `#limitTip` is absolutely positioned but has no positioned ancestor, so it lands at (500,1170) instead of under the '?' button — the user sees nothing appear. Edit 1 makes the existing `.row` wrapper (which exists solely to hold the trigger) the containing block and shrink-wraps it; edit 2 moves the tooltip inside that wrapper and out of the <label> (a <span> rather than a <div> keeps the phrasing-content nesting valid; the id, role=tooltip and aria-describedby wiring are unchanged). No JS changes: the setTimeout(...,4000) auto-dismiss that the case is about is preserved, so expected stays 'failed'. Verified on a scratch copy by re-running probe-case.js and by a timed computed-style check. The .md needs no change (it does not describe the tooltip's coordinates).

One incidental corpus-hygiene note, unrelated to the complaint: this page ships `<body data-intended-classification="inapplicable" data-sc="4.1.3">` (L36) plus a visible `.why` block explaining the answer — both leak the expected outcome to anyone (or any model) reading the served HTML.

cases.evidence: result.json L280-288 describes an 'E-commerce running-shoe store' per-keystroke counter with primarySelector `p#liveCount[role="alert"]`, cited against the Understanding 'too chatty' passage. The shipped page is Notification preferences — Helmsley Workspace; its live element is L72: ``, filled with 'Preferences saved.' by the submit handler (L94-101). `grep -c p#liveCount` over the page: 0 matches; there is no search input and no role=alert anywhere. The case's own .md is already rewritten to the Helmsley/F103 scenario and its 'Notes on the dispute this case resolves' (L100-115) records that the old role=alert scenario was rejected by an adversarial reviewer and replaced.
cases.reasoning: Davin's comment is right on the substance: the element does not have a wrong urgency, it has no announcing politeness at all (aria-live='off', no role=status/alert/log, not an <output>). The mismatch is purely stale metadata — the .md, the page and the F103 citation all agree with each other, and `expected` remains 'failed' either way, so no ground-truth call is involved. The patch rewrites scenario/mechanism/primarySelector/whyAutomatedToolsMiss/citation in the source of truth to the fixture that actually ships. The corpus's DRIFT-REPORT.md already lists this case as not-aligned for the same reason.

proposedFix.rationale: aspectResults[wrong-live-region-politeness-for-urgency].built.pages[case-01] still carries the pre-rewrite running-shoe scenario, whose primarySelector p#liveCount[role="alert"] matches nothing in the shipped page. Replace scenario/mechanism/primarySelector/whyAutomatedToolsMiss/citation with the Helmsley aria-live="off" / F103 case that the HTML and the .md both describe; `expected` is unchanged at 'failed'. Verified: the oldString occurs exactly once and the file still parses as JSON after the replacement. The .md needs no change — it already documents this scenario. manifest.json is generated from result.json and must be regenerated afterwards (it currently carries the same stale text).

edits.oldString:
"scenario": "E-commerce running-shoe store with an instant search filter: a 'N results' counter beneath the search box updates on every keystroke. The counter is a present, valid live region wired role=alert (assertive), so typing 'shoes' fires five assertive announcements in under a second, each interrupting and clobbering the last. A low-value, high-frequency count should be polite (role=status), not assertive.",
            "expected": "failed",
            "mechanism": "role=alert maps to an assertive live region: each text change interrupts current speech. The region's text is replaced on every 'input' event, so a per-keystroke result count repeatedly preempts whatever the screen reader was reading and cuts off its own prior announcements. The message is announced (absence-checkers pass) but at a politeness inappropriate for its low value and high cadence — the 'too chatty' failure.",
            "primarySelector": "p#liveCount[role=\"alert\"]",
            "whyAutomatedToolsMiss": "A non-empty live region is present at load with role=alert + aria-atomic=true and genuinely announces. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only that a status message CAN be announced; both assertive and polite are legal values, so no rule fires. No static or single-snapshot scan can weigh that a count firing on every keystroke is low-value, high-cadence content that should be polite — that needs human understanding of the message's meaning and frequency.",
            "citation": {
              "doc": "WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 4.1.3 Status Messages — 'Other uses of live regions or alerts' (wcag-understanding/status-messages.html)",
              "quote": "Live regions and alerts can be usefully applied in many situations where a change of content takes place which does not constitute a status message, as defined in this success criterion. However, there is a risk of making an application too \"chatty\" for a screen reader user. User testing should be carried out to ensure the appropriate level of feedback is achieved."
            }
edits.newString:
"scenario": "Team-workspace SaaS ('Helmsley Workspace') notification-preferences page: pressing 'Save preferences' reveals a green 'Preferences saved.' banner beside the button. The banner is wired aria-live='off' with aria-atomic='true', carries no role=status/alert/log and is not an <output>, so the live-region wiring looks present to a linter while the value 'off' tells assistive technology to ignore the update. Sighted users see the confirmation; screen-reader users hear nothing and cannot tell whether the save succeeded.",
            "expected": "failed",
            "mechanism": "The post-submit text 'Preferences saved.' meets the status-message definition — it does not take focus and it reports the success of the user's action — but the only live property on the region is aria-live='off', which is neither 'polite' nor 'assertive' and suppresses announcement entirely. With no role=status/alert/log and no <output> element, none of F103's enumerated techniques is present, so the message is never programmatically surfaced. The politeness value is not merely too chatty for the message's urgency; it is silence.",
            "primarySelector": "span#savedMsg[aria-live=\"off\"]",
            "whyAutomatedToolsMiss": "The element carries an aria-live attribute and aria-atomic='true', so a static scan sees a live-region-shaped element and nothing malformed — 'off' is a syntactically valid aria-live token, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not flag it. The banner is also empty in the load-time DOM, so no content rule has any text to inspect. Recognising that 'Preferences saved.' is a status message, and that 'off' suppresses its announcement, requires submitting the form and reasoning about the politeness value — a behavioural, human-in-the-loop judgment no point-in-time scan makes.",
            "citation": {
              "doc": "WCAG Techniques — F103 'Failure of Success Criterion 4.1.3 due to providing status messages that cannot be programmatically determined through role or properties' (wcag-techniques/failures/F103.html)",
              "quote": "The absence of all of these techniques predicts a failure for the status message be announced to the user."
            }
